You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Great Fish (Sea-monster)

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching the 'great fish' (Jonah 1:17) is read primarily as a type or foreshadowing of Christ's death, burial, and resurrection: Jonah's three days and nights in the fish's belly prefigure Christ's three days in the tomb (the 'sign of Jonah'). Closely bound up with this, the fish itself is understood as an instrument of God's providence — simultaneously an agent of divine judgment/discipline and the appointed means of deliverance for the disobedient prophet.",

    "Jonah 1:17",
    "Jonah 2:1-10",
    "Matthew 12:39-41",

    "Luke 11:29-30"

        "Jonah 2:2",
        "Jonah 2:6",
        "Psalm 88:3-6"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The great fish/sea-monster as the biblical chaos monster (Leviathan, Rahab, tannin), symbolizing the powers of chaos, evil, or Satan that God subdues; some patristic and later interpreters connected Jonah's fish to this motif, reading the swallowing as engulfment by demonic or hostile power.",

        "Isaiah 27:1",

        "Job 41",

        "Jeremiah 51:34",

        "Jonah read allegorically as Israel"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The fish carries no fixed symbolic meaning at all; it is a narrative or didactic device (a 'prop' God 'appoints,' like the plant, worm, and wind in Jonah 4) within a parabolic or satirical story, and pressing it for symbolism misreads the genre. Common in modern critical scholarship.",
      "basis": [
        "Jonah 1:17 ('the LORD appointed')",
        "Jonah 4:6-8 (parallel appointed agents)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The fish as a symbol of baptism or salvific rebirth — being swallowed and cast out alive as a figure of dying and rising with Christ through the waters; appears in some patristic homilies and early Christian funerary art (Jonah cycles in the catacombs), where the fish scene signifies resurrection hope.",
      "basis": [
        "Jonah 2:10",
        "Romans 6:3-4 (applied typologically)",
        "1 Peter 3:20-21 (analogous water-deliverance typology)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "The Christological typology is unusually well anchored because Jesus himself makes the connection explicit in Matthew 12:39-40, so the 'sign of Jonah' reading (burial and resurrection of Christ) is dominant across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions and in patristic sources (e.g., Justin Martyr, Cyril of Jerusalem, Jerome, Augustine). The Sheol/death reading is largely complementary to it. Note that the Hebrew calls it a 'great fish' (dag gadol), not a whale or monster; the 'sea-monster' framing comes from the Septuagint's kētos (echoed in Matthew 12:40), which is what invites the Leviathan/chaos-monster comparisons. If the author's term 'sea-monster' is meant to align the fish with chaos/Leviathan or with Satan, that is a recognizable but minority strand, not the mainstream consensus."
}

BOOK ENTRY
A great ruler among the sea of peoples — the personal head who can stand for the kingdom, state, and administration acting through him. Pharaoh stands for Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar for Babylon, and Caesar for Rome: the ruler swallows through the body he heads, and is forced to give back what he swallowed.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: God's appointed rescue-instrument, a type of the three days in the tomb.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Ezek 29:3; 32:2; Jer 51:34, 44; Dan 7:17, 23; John 19:15-16) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Ezekiel 29:3 — Speak, and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers, which hath said, My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself.
Ezekiel 32:2 — Son of man, take up a lamentation for Pharaoh king of Egypt, and say unto him, Thou art like a young lion of the nations, and thou art as a whale in the seas: and thou camest forth with thy rivers, and troubledst the waters with thy feet, and fouledst their rivers.
Jeremiah 51:34 — Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon hath devoured me, he hath crushed me, he hath made me an empty vessel, he hath swallowed me up like a dragon, he hath filled his belly with my delicates, he hath cast me out.
Jeremiah 51:44 — And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and I will bring forth out of his mouth that which he hath swallowed up: and the nations shall not flow together any more unto him: yea, the wall of Babylon shall fall.
Daniel 7:17 — These great beasts, which are four, are four kings, which shall arise out of the earth.
Daniel 7:23 — Thus he said, The fourth beast shall be the fourth kingdom upon earth, which shall be diverse from all kingdoms, and shall devour the whole earth, and shall tread it down, and break it in pieces.
John 19:15 — But they cried out, Away with him, away with him, crucify him. Pilate saith unto them, Shall I crucify your King? The chief priests answered, We have no king but Caesar.
John 19:16 — Then delivered he him therefore unto them to be crucified. And they took Jesus, and led him away.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
